whyItExists.problem: You need to verify data integrity without storing the full data, detect file tampering, and create unique fingerprints for large datasets.
whyItExists.solution: Cryptographic hash functions produce a fixed-size digest that acts as a data fingerprint. Any change to the input produces a completely different output.
whyItExists.whenToUse: File integrity checks, digital signatures (sign the hash not the data), content addressing (Git, IPFS), data deduplication.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Password storage (use bcrypt/Argon2 instead — SHA-256 is too fast). Encrypting data (hashing is one-way, not reversible).

explainModes.beginner: A hash function is like a fingerprint scanner for data. The same file always gives the same fingerprint, but you cannot reconstruct the file from the fingerprint.
explainModes.simple: It converts any amount of data into a fixed-length string. If even one byte changes, the hash changes completely — this is called the avalanche effect.
explainModes.standard: Cryptographic hash functions must be: deterministic, fast to compute, one-way (preimage resistant), second-preimage resistant, and collision resistant. SHA-256 produces 32 bytes; SHA-3-256 also produces 32 bytes but uses a different internal structure.
explainModes.technical: SHA-256 uses a Merkle-Damgård construction with 64 rounds of bitwise operations. SHA-3 uses a Keccak sponge construction, making it structurally different from SHA-2 and immune to length-extension attacks.
explainModes.deepDive: Length-extension attacks exploit Merkle-Damgård: given hash(msg), you can compute hash(msg || padding || extra) without knowing msg. HMAC prevents this. SHA-3 (Keccak) is immune by design. For keyed hashing, always use HMAC-SHA256 or BLAKE2 — never bare SHA256(key || msg).

content.text: A cryptographic hash function takes any input and produces a fixed-size output (digest). Every good hash function satisfies five properties: deterministic, fast, preimage resistant (one-way), second-preimage resistant, and collision resistant.

items: Deterministic — same input always produces same output
Avalanche effect — tiny input change flips ~50% of output bits
Preimage resistant — given hash(x), cannot find x
Second-preimage resistant — given x, cannot find y≠x with hash(y)=hash(x)
Collision resistant — cannot find any two inputs with the same hash

content.definition: It must be computationally infeasible to find two different inputs that produce the same hash. MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collisions; SHA-256 does not.

content.code:
import hashlib
import hmac

# --- SHA-256: standard choice ---
data = b"Important document content"
hash_sha256 = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
print("SHA-256:", hash_sha256)  # 32 bytes = 64 hex chars

# --- SHA-3: modern alternative ---
hash_sha3 = hashlib.sha3_256(data).hexdigest()
print("SHA3-256:", hash_sha3)

# --- BLAKE2b: fastest option, good for checksums ---
hash_blake = hashlib.blake2b(data, digest_size=32).hexdigest()
print("BLAKE2b:", hash_blake)

# --- HMAC: keyed hash for message authentication ---
key = b"my_secret_key"
mac = hmac.new(key=key, msg=data, digestmod="sha256")
print("HMAC-SHA256:", mac.hexdigest())

# --- File integrity check ---
def sha256_file(path: str) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()

# --- WRONG: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken ---
# hashlib.md5(data)   # broken for security, avoid
# hashlib.sha1(data)  # collision attacks proven, avoid

content.text: MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collision attacks. Never use them for security. Use SHA-256, SHA-3-256, or BLAKE2 at minimum. Never use SHA-256 to store passwords — use Argon2id or bcrypt.

a.name: SHA-256
a.description: SHA-2 family, Merkle-Damgård construction, NIST standard
weaknesses: Same family as SHA-1 (different math but same design)
a.useWhen: General purpose: TLS, certificates, Git, file integrity

b.name: SHA-3-256
b.description: Keccak sponge construction, completely different design from SHA-2
strengths: Structurally different from SHA-2 (hedge against SHA-2 breaks)
b.useWhen: New protocols, Ethereum, when you want design diversity

content.text: A plain hash authenticates data but not who sent it. HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) combines a hash with a secret key to prove both integrity and origin.

content.code:
import hmac, hashlib, os

key = os.urandom(32)  # shared secret between sender and receiver
message = b"Transfer $1000 to account 9876"

# Sender computes MAC
my_mac = hmac.new(key=key, msg=message, digestmod="sha256").hexdigest()

# Receiver verifies (constant-time comparison)
received_mac = my_mac  # from the message packet
if hmac.compare_digest(my_mac, received_mac):
    print("Message is authentic")
else:
    print("Message was tampered!")

content.text: Use HMAC-SHA256 for API request signing, webhook verification, and cookie integrity checks. It prevents length-extension attacks that bare SHA-256 is vulnerable to.

questions.question: What is a preimage attack?
options: Finding two inputs with the same hash
Finding the input from a known hash output
questions.explanation: A preimage attack tries to find an input M such that hash(M) equals a known hash — reversing the hash function.

questions.question: Why should you NOT use SHA-256 to store passwords?
options: SHA-256 produces hashes that are too long
SHA-256 is too fast — attackers can try billions of guesses per second
SHA-256 is not supported on most systems
SHA-256 adds automatic salting that interferes with login
questions.explanation: SHA-256 is designed to be fast. An attacker with a GPU can try ~10 billion SHA-256 hashes per second, making offline brute force trivial. Use Argon2id.

questions.question: What does HMAC add to a regular hash?
options: Authentication — proves the message came from someone with the secret key
Compression of the data before hashing
questions.explanation: HMAC uses a secret key to authenticate both the data and its origin. Without the key, an attacker cannot forge a valid MAC.

faq.q: Can I use SHA-256 to store passwords?
faq.a: No. SHA-256 is too fast — an attacker can try billions of guesses per second on a GPU. Use bcrypt, Argon2id, or scrypt, which are intentionally slow and memory-intensive.
With SHA-256 (Merkle-Damgård construction), given hash(msg), an attacker can compute hash(msg || extra_data) without knowing the original msg. HMAC prevents this by double-wrapping the key.

faq.q: What is the best hash algorithm to use today?
faq.a: SHA-256 for general use; SHA-3-256 for new protocols where design diversity matters; BLAKE2 for high-performance hashing. SHA-1 and MD5 must not be used for security.

examples: Git identifies every commit, file, and tree by its SHA-1 hash (migrating to SHA-256)
AWS uses HMAC-SHA256 to sign API requests and verify they were not tampered with in transit
Package managers (pip, npm) publish SHA-256 checksums to verify downloaded packages
